transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because my sleep has been really disrupted. I’m normally very disciplined about sleep, but since my cousin died, I lie awake replaying that night. Then I wake up around 3 or 4 in the morning with these bits of hospital images in my head, and I’m going into board meetings feeling like I’ve only slept in pieces.
Do you have memories or thoughts about your cousin's death that keep popping into your mind throughout the day?

Yes. It’s not constant, but it does happen. At odd moments, like if a phone rings late or I’m driving and headlights hit me a certain way, I suddenly see the hospital corridor in my mind, or I hear the police officer’s voice again. It sort of pushes in, and I have to stop for a moment and steady myself.
Have you been avoiding people, places, or activities since your cousin's death?

I’m not sure I’d say I’m avoiding things. I’ve still been going to work and handling what I need to handle. I may be a little less eager to be around people, but I haven’t really noticed myself steering clear of specific places or activities.
Do you feel guilty about your cousin's death?
I don’t think so. I mean, I feel awful that it happened, but I haven’t really been blaming myself for his death. It’s more sadness and shock than guilt.
Have you experienced a decrease in interest or pleasure in activities you normally enjoy since your cousin's death?

Yes, I think so. I’ve still been showing up and doing what’s expected, but I don’t really feel much from things that should comfort me. At the prayer gatherings, or when my nieces tried to hug me or say something kind, I behaved normally, but inside I didn’t feel warmth or relief. It’s like that part of me has gone quiet.
Have you noticed any change in your appetite since your cousin's death?
I haven’t really noticed a clear change. I’m eating more or less like usual, I think. Maybe some meals feel a bit mechanical, but my appetite hasn’t stood out to me as different.
Have you found it difficult to function at work or in your daily life since your cousin's death?

Yes. I’m still going to the most essential meetings, but I’m not functioning at my usual level. I’ve had to hand off some community obligations and shorten my workdays because I don’t feel as steady or as effective with people as I normally am.
Do you feel like you're struggling to connect with others or maintain your usual relationships since your cousin's death?

Yes. I’m still around people and doing what I’m supposed to do, but I don’t feel connected the way I normally would. At the prayer gatherings, and even when my nieces were trying to comfort me, I responded properly, but inside there wasn’t much warmth or relief. It feels like that affectionate part of me has gone quiet.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings and changes since your cousin's death?
About three weeks now. It started that night, when my cousin died in the highway collision, and it’s just been going on since then.
Would you say that this feeling of not feeling warmth or relief from things that should comfort you is something that happens occasionally or is it more of a constant state for you now?

It’s more constant now. I can act the way I’m supposed to, like at the prayer gatherings or when my nieces try to comfort me, but inside I don’t really feel warmth or relief. It’s like that part of me has gone quiet.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or feeling restless and unable to sit still since your cousin's death?
I haven’t really noticed that, no. I don’t think I’m moving or talking much slower than usual, and I wouldn’t say I’m pacing or unable to sit still. I’m just… going through the motions.
Do you feel like you're under a lot of emotional pain or distress most of the time since your cousin's death?
I’m not sure I’d say most of the time. I’m upset, yes, and it comes in waves, but I haven’t really thought of it as constant emotional pain. It’s just been hard.
Are there activities that you usually find enjoyable or fulfilling, but since your cousin's death, you've found yourself not wanting to do them?

Yes. At the prayer gatherings, or even when my nieces tried to comfort me, I went through the motions and acted the way I should. But I didn’t really feel any warmth or relief from it. It was like the part of me that would normally feel affection or comfort just wasn’t there.
Have you felt like you're moving or speaking slower than you used to?
No, I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed myself moving or talking slower than usual.
Have you felt like you're restless and can't sit still since your cousin's death?
Not really. I mean, I’ve been unsettled at times, but I haven’t noticed that I can’t sit still or that kind of restlessness.
Would you describe yourself as feeling empty or numb most of the time since your cousin's death?

Yes… numb is probably the right word. I’ve been doing what I’m supposed to do, like at the prayer gatherings, and when my nieces try to comfort me. But inside I don’t really feel warmth or relief. It’s like that affectionate part of me has just gone quiet.
Have you felt like you're moving or speaking slower than you used to, or have you had trouble sitting still?
I don’t think so. I know you asked something similar before, and no—I haven’t noticed myself moving or talking slower, and I’m not really pacing around or unable to sit still either.
Have your symptoms lasted for more than two weeks?
Yes. It’s been about three weeks now, since the night my cousin died in that highway collision.
Have you felt like you're moving or talking slower than usual, or have you had trouble sitting still, in the last few weeks?
I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed myself moving or talking slower, and I’m not especially restless or unable to sit still.
Would you say that the feeling of not enjoying things you used to is something that happens with most activities now?

Yes, I think so. Even when people are trying to comfort me—like at the prayer gatherings, or when my nieces were being affectionate—I can act the way I’m supposed to, but inside I don’t really feel warmth or relief. It’s like that part of me has gone quiet.
